Think about a server that needs growing user storage—LVM lets you expand without reformatting. Ready to begin? Notice the three key topics highlighted to guide your practice.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives define practical competence for storage administration. First, you will understand how to partition, format, and mount storage so that new disks become usable. That means you can take a raw device, create a partition table and partition, apply a filesystem, and mount it for immediate use. Second, you will configure persistent mounts using the /etc/fstab file: you’ll learn to use UUIDs, set appropriate mount options, and validate entries safely using mount -a. Third, you will explain the benefits and core concepts of Logical Volume Management. You should be able to describe physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes and why LVM simplifies resizing and snapshot workflows. Fourth, you will perform basic LVM operations: initialize PVs, create a VG, carve out LVs, format them, mount them, and extend LVs when needed. Each objective emphasizes safety: always double-check device names and back up fstab before editing. Together these skills let you add persistent, resizable storage to servers with minimal downtime.

screens.title: Partitioning: dividing physical disks
screens.narratorSegment: Partitioning is the act of dividing a physical disk into one or more logical sections that the operating system treats independently. Each partition holds a filesystem or can be used for swap or LVM. The two common partition table schemes are MBR and GPT; MBR is older and limited, while GPT supports larger disks and more partitions. In practice you will use fdisk for MBR or smaller drives and gdisk for GPT-managed disks. A safe workflow is to first identify the device with lsblk, then run fdisk or gdisk on the correct device name. Inside fdisk you create a new partition with the new command, set the type if needed, and write changes. Always double-check the device path before writing because fdisk will alter the disk metadata and risk data loss on the wrong drive. Example: when attaching a new virtual disk /dev/sdb, create /dev/sdb1 and mark it type 8e if you intend to use it with LVM. A common misconception is that every disk must be partitioned; you can use an entire disk directly, but partitions provide flexibility and standard device names. Takeaway: partitioning prepares storage units but is a potentially destructive operation—confirm devices and back up data.

content.html:
Core Concept Partitioning
Divide a disk into usable sections
Use fdisk or gdisk. Confirm device names and choose type appropriately.
Definition and rules
  • Partition: a logical section of a physical disk with its own metadata.
  • Partition table: MBR or GPT; GPT supports larger disks and many partitions.
  • Tools: fdisk for MBR-style, gdisk for GPT. Always run lsblk first.
  • Tip: mark partitions as type 8e for LVM usage when planning LVM.
Common misconception
You must partition every disk. You can use whole-disk devices directly, but partitioning is safer and more standard.
Example walkthrough (visualized)
Attach virtual disk /dev/sdb, confirm with lsblk, then run fdisk /dev/sdb. Use n to create a partition and w to write changes. Label type 8e for LVM if needed.
Check device before you write
# List block devices and sizes
lsblk

# Then partition the new disk
sudo fdisk /dev/sdb
# Inside fdisk: n p 1 Enter Enter t 8e w
Why partitions matter: isolation and management
When to use GPT: large disks and many partitions
Safety: always confirm device and backup important data

screens.title: Partitioning in the terminal: fdisk demo
screens.narratorSegment: In this practical demonstration we’ll run the common sequence to partition a new disk. First identify the device using lsblk or blkid; this prevents writing partitions to the wrong disk. For example, you might see a new device named /dev/sdb with no partitions. Run sudo fdisk /dev/sdb to enter the fdisk prompt. Inside fdisk the typical commands are: n to create a new partition, p to print the partition table, t to change type, and w to write changes. If you plan to use LVM, change the type to the LVM code so downstream tools recognize it. After writing, re-run lsblk to confirm that /dev/sdb1 exists. A concrete example: create partition 1, accept default sector values to use the whole disk, set type to LVM, and write. A common mistake is forgetting to refresh kernel partition information before using the device; if needed, run partprobe or reboot. Takeaway: the interactive fdisk flow is quick but destructive if you target the wrong device—always verify first. Now, let’s look at the exact commands you’ll use in the terminal so you can practice safely.

keyIdea.title: fdisk flow
keyIdea.text: Use lsblk first, then fdisk with n, p, t, and w; confirm new partition exists before formatting.

content.html:
Process fdisk terminal demo
Partition a new disk interactively
Confirm devices, use fdisk commands, then verify partitions.
Step-by-step commands
# List devices
lsblk

# Start fdisk on the new disk
sudo fdisk /dev/sdb
# Inside fdisk: n (new) -> p (primary) -> 1 -> Enter -> Enter
# t -> 8e (set partition type to LVM) -> w (write)
If the kernel does not see the new partition, run sudo partprobe or re-run lsblk after a short pause.
Verification and common mistake
  • Verify with lsblk or sudo fdisk -l /dev/sdb.
  • Don’t run fdisk on the wrong device; confirm sizes and mount points first.
  • If a system is using GPT and you use fdisk, prefer gdisk instead to avoid compatibility issues.
Pro tip
When scripting partitioning, use parted for non-interactive operations and ensure device checks are in place.

screens.title: Filesystems: structure and common choices
screens.narratorSegment: A filesystem defines how files, directories, and metadata are organized on a partition. It provides indexing, directory structures, journaling for integrity, and optional features like snapshots or built-in RAID. ext4 is the common default: it is stable and supports journaling, making it a safe choice for many servers. XFS is often chosen for very large filesystems and workloads that need high throughput for large files. Btrfs is newer and offers advanced features such as snapshots and checksums but can be more complex. The right choice depends on your workload: ext4 for general purpose, XFS for large-scale storage needs, and Btrfs when you need snapshotting or advanced features. A misconception is that one filesystem is best for all cases; performance and feature trade-offs matter. Example: a web server with many small files typically uses ext4, while a media server handling very large files may use XFS. Always consider support and tooling in your distribution, and remember you can mix filesystems across different partitions or logical volumes to match each workload. The core takeaway is to match filesystem features to your operational needs and test before deploying to production.

Definition Filesystem choices
How files are organized on disk
Choose a filesystem based on features, performance, and operational needs.
Filesystem roles and features
  • Journaling: improves integrity after crashes (ext4, XFS).
  • Snapshots: point-in-time copies (Btrfs).
  • Scalability: capacity and performance differences (XFS for large files).
  • Tooling: check distro support and recovery tools.
Comparison at a glance
ext4
Reliable default, journaling, good for many workloads.
XFS
High performance for large files and large filesystems.
Btrfs
Snapshots and advanced features; test before production.
Example: Small web files → ext4
Example: Media server large files → XFS
Example: Need snapshots → Btrfs

screens.title: Formatting a partition and quick mkfs examples
screens.narratorSegment: After creating a partition, you must format it with a filesystem before use. The mkfs tool family applies a chosen filesystem to a partition. For example, to format /dev/sdb1 with ext4 you run mkfs. ext4 on that device. After formatting, use blkid to obtain the device’s UUID and use df -h to confirm mount space once mounted. A concrete example workflow: mkfs. ext4 /dev/sdb1, then sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 to capture the UUID. A common mistake is running mkfs on the wrong partition or an already-mounted partition; formatting will destroy existing data and may break mounted services. Always ensure the target is unmounted and the device is the intended one. Another useful command is tune2fs for ext filesystems to adjust options after formatting. Example: when you make a logical volume in LVM, treat the device path /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv like a partition: format it with mkfs. ext4, create a mount point, and mount it. Takeaway: formatting converts raw partition space into a usable filesystem—do it cautiously and verify identifiers afterward. Formatting a partition and quick mkfs examples means use mkfs to apply a filesystem and blkid to capture uuids; never format the wrong device and avoid formatting mounted devices.. In practical terms, apply a filesystem to a partition and verify with blkid and df. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Formatting
Apply a filesystem using mkfs
Format partitions or logical volumes, then record UUIDs for fstab.
Commands you will run
# Format a partition as ext4
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1

# Get the UUID to use in fstab
sudo blkid /dev/sdb1

# Example for a logical volume
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/data_vg/web_lv
sudo mkdir -p /var/www/html_data
sudo mount /dev/data_vg/web_lv /var/www/html_data
# Verify mount
df -h /var/www/html_data
Checks and cautions
  • Ensure the device is not mounted before running mkfs.
  • Confirm the device path using lsblk to avoid data loss.
  • Record the UUID immediately after formatting for fstab entries.
Key takeaway
Formatting makes storage usable; always verify the target and capture the UUID for persistence.

screens.title: Mounting and unmounting filesystems
screens.narratorSegment: Mounting attaches a formatted filesystem to a directory so processes can read and write files there. The mount command takes a device path and a mount point. For example, create a directory such as /mnt/data and run mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data to access that filesystem immediately. To unmount use umount and the mount point or device. A frequent issue when unmounting is the target being busy; processes or shells may still have working directories inside the mount point. Use lsof or fuser to find what is holding files open before attempting to unmount. Another practical approach is to stop services that use the mount, close shells, and then unmount. A common misconception is that umount will force-close access; it will not terminate processes by default. Also use df -h to inspect current usage and mounts and check /proc/mounts for the kernel’s view. For temporary mounts this sequence is sufficient, but for persistent mounts you will later add entries to /etc/fstab. Takeaway: mounting is simple, but unmounting safely requires confirmation no process is using the filesystem so you don’t interrupt active work or corrupt data.

keyIdea.text: Use mount and umount for temporary access; verify no processes are using the mount before unmounting to avoid errors and data inconsistency.

content.html:
Process Flow Mount / Unmount
Attach a filesystem to the directory tree
Use mount for temporary access and check busy processes before unmounting.
Mount commands and checks
# Create mount point and mount
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data

# Check mounts and usage
df -h
cat /proc/mounts
If umount reports busy, run lsof +f -- /mnt/data or sudo fuser -m /mnt/data to find processes.
Example scenario
You mounted /dev/sdb1 to /mnt/data. A backup job runs and holds files open; attempting umount /mnt/data returns device busy. Use lsof to identify the backup process, stop it, then unmount safely.
Common mistake
Trying to unmount while shells or services still use the directory; confirm with lsof or fuser first.

screens.title: Persistent mounts with /etc/fstab
screens.narratorSegment: The /etc/fstab file configures persistent mounts that the system mounts automatically at boot. Each fstab line includes the device (ideally referenced by UUID), the mount point, filesystem type, mount options, dump, and pass number for fsck. Using UUIDs avoids device-name drift when disks reorder. To get a device UUID use blkid and copy the UUID exactly into fstab. An example fstab entry uses the device UUID, mount point such as /data, ext4 as the filesystem, defaults as options, and 0 2 for dump and fsck order. After editing fstab, always back up the file and test your changes with mount -a to attempt mounting all entries without rebooting. If mount -a returns errors, fix them before reboot. A typical error is a wrong filesystem type or a missing mount point directory. A serious consequence of a bad fstab line is a failed boot that drops the system into emergency mode. The standard recovery is to boot into rescue mode, mount the root volume, and fix or comment out the problematic line. Takeaway: prefer UUIDs, test with mount -a, and keep a backup to safeguard boot behavior.

content.html:
Definition /etc/fstab
Configure persistent mounts
Use UUIDs and mount -a to validate entries safely.
Typical fstab entry
# Example fstab line
UUID=abcdef12-3456-7890-abcd-ef1234567890 /data ext4 defaults 0 2
Get the UUID with sudo blkid /dev/data_vg/web_lv or /dev/sdb1 and paste it into fstab to prevent device name issues.
Testing and recovery
  • Back up /etc/fstab before edits: sudo cp /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.bak.
  • Test entries with sudo mount -a to catch errors immediately.
  • If boot fails, use a rescue environment to correct fstab or comment out the bad line.
Common boot problem
A wrong fstab line will halt the boot process. Use a rescue shell to mount root and fix fstab.

screens.title: Introduction to Logical Volume Management (LVM)
screens.narratorSegment: Logical Volume Management, or LVM, is a layer of abstraction between physical storage and the block devices you format and mount. Instead of fixed partitions, LVM lets you pool physical volumes into a volume group and then carve logical volumes out of that pool. The three core terms to remember are Physical Volume, Volume Group, and Logical Volume. A Physical Volume is a disk or partition initialized for LVM use. You combine one or more PVs into a Volume Group, which acts like a storage pool. From that pool you create Logical Volumes, which behave like regular block devices that you can format and mount. The major benefits are flexibility: you can extend logical volumes without taking them offline, create snapshots for backups, and span storage across multiple disks. A common misconception is that LVM is mandatory; it is optional but valuable when you expect capacity changes. Example: if you have two physical disks, you can add both as PVs to one VG and then create a large LV that uses space from both disks. Takeaway: LVM trades a layer of complexity for powerful online resizing and pooling capabilities—learn the PV→VG→LV relationship to manage it confidently.

narration.text: Logical Volume Management, or LVM, is a layer of abstraction between physical storage and the block devices you format and mount. Instead of fixed partitions, LVM lets you pool physical volumes into a volume group and then carve logical volumes out of that pool. The three core terms to remember are Physical Volume, Volume Group, and Logical Volume. A Physical Volume is a disk or partition initialized for LVM use. You combine one or more PVs into a Volume Group, which acts like a storage pool. From that pool you create Logical Volumes, which behave like regular block devices that you can format and mount. The major benefits are flexibility: you can extend logical volumes without taking them offline, create snapshots for backups, and span storage across multiple disks. A common misconception is that LVM is mandatory; it is optional but valuable when you expect capacity changes. Example: if you have two physical disks, you can add both as PVs to one VG and then create a large LV that uses space from both disks. Takeaway: LVM trades a layer of complexity for powerful online resizing and pooling capabilities—learn the PV→VG→LV relationship to manage it confidently.

keyIdea.text: PV → VG → LV: pool physical storage into groups and carve logical volumes for flexible, resizable storage.

content.html:
Core Concept LVM fundamentals
PV, VG, LV explained
Pool disks with PVs, create VGs, and carve LVs that act like partitions.
Component definitions
  • Physical Volume (PV): a disk or partition initialized with pvcreate.
  • Volume Group (VG): a pool of PVs created with vgcreate.
  • Logical Volume (LV): a resizable block device made with lvcreate.
Why use LVM?
Benefits include online resizing, snapshots, and the ability to span storage across disks. It adds management complexity but enables growth without repartitioning.
Example: Combine /dev/sdb1 and /dev/sdc1 into one VG to hold user data.
Misconception: LVM is required. It’s optional but useful when flexible resizing matters.

screens.title: LVM hands-on: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough covers the exact sequence to create an LVM-backed filesystem you can mount. Start by creating partitions and marking them for LVM, then initialize with pvcreate. For example: sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 initializes two physical volumes. Next create a volume group with sudo vgcreate my_vg /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1. From that group, create a logical volume: sudo lvcreate -L 100G -n user_data_lv my_vg. This yields a device node such as /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv. Format this logical volume with mkfs. ext4, create a mount point, and mount it like any other filesystem. A concrete example: create a 5GB logical volume for a web directory and mount it at /var/www/html_data. A frequent misconception is that you must create equal-sized LVs; you can create many LVs of varying sizes and later extend them as long as there is free space in the VG. Always ensure to run vgdisplay and lvdisplay to confirm capacities before extending or creating LVs. Takeaway: pvcreate, vgcreate, and lvcreate form the basic LVM workflow—practice on non-production systems first and back up important data. LVM hands-on: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate means pvcreate initializes disks, vgcreate pools them, and lvcreate creates logical volumes you can format and mount.. In practical terms, create pvs, make a vg, and carve a small lv for application data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process LVM build
Create PV → VG → LV
Example commands for a simple LVM-backed mount.
Commands
# Initialize physical volumes
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1

# Create a volume group
sudo vgcreate my_vg /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1

# Create a 5GB logical volume
sudo lvcreate -L 5G -n web_lv my_vg

# Format and mount
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/my_vg/web_lv
sudo mkdir -p /var/www/html_data
sudo mount /dev/my_vg/web_lv /var/www/html_data
Checks and best practices
  • Confirm PVs with sudo pvs and VG with sudo vgs before creating LVs.
  • Use lvdisplay to see the LV path used for formatting and fstab entries.
  • Back up critical data before performing LVM operations on existing volumes.
Example scenario
Create a web LV, format it, mount it to serve static files. Later extend it if traffic grows.

screens.title: Extending and resizing LVM volumes
screens.narratorSegment: One of LVM’s most valuable features is online resizing. If your volume group has free extents, you can extend a logical volume and then resize its filesystem. The typical sequence is lvextend followed by resize2fs for ext filesystems or xfs_growfs for XFS. For example, to add 50GB to user_data_lv run lvextend -L +50G /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv. After lvextend, resize the filesystem so the OS can use the new space: run sudo resize2fs /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv for ext4. A concrete example: a user_data_lv running out of space can be extended while the system continues to serve files, avoiding lengthy downtime. Misconceptions include assuming every filesystem supports online resize—XFS can only be grown while mounted, and some older filesystems cannot be resized online. Always check free space in the VG with vgs and ensure backups exist before resizing operations. If the VG lacks free space, add a new PV to the VG with pvcreate and vgextend, then repeat the lvextend step. Takeaway: LVM enables safe growth, but the filesystem tool matters; confirm the filesystem type and available VG space before resizing. Extending and resizing LVM volumes means use lvextend then the appropriate filesystem grow tool; confirm vg free space and filesystem support for online resizing.. In practical terms, grow logical volumes and resize filesystems without long downtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use lvextend then the appropriate filesystem grow tool; confirm VG free space and filesystem support for online resizing.

content.html:
Process LVM resizing
Extend LVs and grow filesystems
lvextend then resize filesystem tools vary by type.
Common commands
# Add space to LV
sudo lvextend -L +50G /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv

# For ext4
sudo resize2fs /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv

# For XFS (grow while mounted)
sudo xfs_growfs /mount/point
Checks and additions
  • Confirm free space in VG with sudo vgs.
  • If no free space, add a PV: sudo pvcreate /dev/sdd1; sudo vgextend my_vg /dev/sdd1.
  • Always back up critical data before major resizing operations.
Practical tip
Test resize operations in a non-production environment to confirm the exact commands your filesystem requires.

screens.title: Troubleshooting common storage issues
screens.narratorSegment: Storage problems often surface as boot failures, busy unmounts, or lack of space when resizing. The most common boot-time failure arises from an incorrect /etc/fstab line. The system attempts to mount everything in fstab during boot; if an entry references a missing device, wrong UUID, or bad filesystem type, the boot process can drop into emergency mode. The standard fix is to boot from rescue media or use a root shell to mount the root filesystem and edit or comment out the offending line, then test with mount -a. Another frequent issue is attempting to unmount while processes still use the mount point. Use lsof or fuser to identify and stop those processes before unmounting. For LVM, running out of free extents in a VG prevents extending LVs; the remedy is to add a new PV to the VG or free space by shrinking other LVs where possible. A key misconception is assuming that a failed mount at boot always means a corrupted filesystem; often it’s an fstab syntax or device naming problem. Example: after adding a new LV and writing an fstab entry with the wrong UUID, the system fails to boot. Recovery involves fixing fstab, testing with mount -a, and rebooting. Takeaway: careful validation and backups drastically reduce recovery time.

Common problems and fixes
Methodical checks prevent escalations and shorten recovery time.
Boot fails after editing fstab
Cause: wrong UUID, incorrect filesystem type, or missing mount point. Fix: boot rescue, mount root, edit /etc/fstab, and test with mount -a before reboot.

Mounting makes a filesystem accessible; use mount and unmount carefully and check df -h and /proc/mounts. These core ideas will help you manage storage reliably and scale it as needs grow.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how to take raw disks and make them useful for Linux systems. We’ll walk through the three steps every administrator follows: partitioning a device, formatting a partition with a filesystem, and mounting that filesystem so it becomes part of the directory tree. You will also learn how to make mounts persistent across reboots using the /etc/fstab file, and why Logical Volume Management, or LVM, can simplify future growth by pooling physical storage into flexible logical volumes. Along the way I’ll show concrete command examples you’ll use in a terminal, point out common mistakes like unmounting a busy mount point or mis-editing fstab, and explain when to choose ext4, XFS, or Btrfs. By the end you should be able to add a new virtual disk, partition it for LVM, create a volume group and logical volume, format it, mount it, and configure persistence. Think about a server that needs growing user storage—LVM lets you expand without reformatting. Ready to begin? Notice the three key topics highlighted to guide your practice.

These four objectives define practical competence for storage administration. First, you will understand how to partition, format, and mount storage so that new disks become usable. That means you can take a raw device, create a partition table and partition, apply a filesystem, and mount it for immediate use. Second, you will configure persistent mounts using the /etc/fstab file: you’ll learn to use UUIDs, set appropriate mount options, and validate entries safely using mount -a. Third, you will explain the benefits and core concepts of Logical Volume Management. You should be able to describe physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes and why LVM simplifies resizing and snapshot workflows. Fourth, you will perform basic LVM operations: initialize PVs, create a VG, carve out LVs, format them, mount them, and extend LVs when needed. Each objective emphasizes safety: always double-check device names and back up fstab before editing. Together these skills let you add persistent, resizable storage to servers with minimal downtime.

Practice is essential. You’ll follow a hands-on scenario that simulates adding a new virtual disk, partitioning it for LVM, creating a volume group, and carving out a logical volume for a web application. You will format that logical volume, mount it, and add an /etc/fstab entry using the volume’s UUID. During practice you’ll learn how to verify mounts with df -h, inspect block identifiers with blkid, and safely test fstab changes with mount -a so the system doesn’t fail to boot. We’ll also cover quick troubleshooting steps you’ll use when a mount point reports as busy or when an fstab entry prevents boot. These exercises focus on command-line workflows that are common in servers and virtual machines where GUI tools aren’t available. Expect to run a short sequence of commands, always confirm device names first, and keep a rescue plan such as a live environment or root shell in case an fstab edit causes an emergency boot. This mindset — practice with careful verification — keeps production systems safe while you gain practical skill.

Partitioning is the act of dividing a physical disk into one or more logical sections that the operating system treats independently. Each partition holds a filesystem or can be used for swap or LVM. The two common partition table schemes are MBR and GPT; MBR is older and limited, while GPT supports larger disks and more partitions. In practice you will use fdisk for MBR or smaller drives and gdisk for GPT-managed disks. A safe workflow is to first identify the device with lsblk, then run fdisk or gdisk on the correct device name. Inside fdisk you create a new partition with the new command, set the type if needed, and write changes. Always double-check the device path before writing because fdisk will alter the disk metadata and risk data loss on the wrong drive. Example: when attaching a new virtual disk /dev/sdb, create /dev/sdb1 and mark it type 8e if you intend to use it with LVM. A common misconception is that every disk must be partitioned; you can use an entire disk directly, but partitions provide flexibility and standard device names. Takeaway: partitioning prepares storage units but is a potentially destructive operation—confirm devices and back up data.

In this practical demonstration we’ll run the common sequence to partition a new disk. First identify the device using lsblk or blkid; this prevents writing partitions to the wrong disk. For example, you might see a new device named /dev/sdb with no partitions. Run sudo fdisk /dev/sdb to enter the fdisk prompt. Inside fdisk the typical commands are: n to create a new partition, p to print the partition table, t to change type, and w to write changes. If you plan to use LVM, change the type to the LVM code so downstream tools recognize it. After writing, re-run lsblk to confirm that /dev/sdb1 exists. A concrete example: create partition 1, accept default sector values to use the whole disk, set type to LVM, and write. A common mistake is forgetting to refresh kernel partition information before using the device; if needed, run partprobe or reboot. Takeaway: the interactive fdisk flow is quick but destructive if you target the wrong device—always verify first. Now, let’s look at the exact commands you’ll use in the terminal so you can practice safely.

A filesystem defines how files, directories, and metadata are organized on a partition. It provides indexing, directory structures, journaling for integrity, and optional features like snapshots or built-in RAID. ext4 is the common default: it is stable and supports journaling, making it a safe choice for many servers. XFS is often chosen for very large filesystems and workloads that need high throughput for large files. Btrfs is newer and offers advanced features such as snapshots and checksums but can be more complex. The right choice depends on your workload: ext4 for general purpose, XFS for large-scale storage needs, and Btrfs when you need snapshotting or advanced features. A misconception is that one filesystem is best for all cases; performance and feature trade-offs matter. Example: a web server with many small files typically uses ext4, while a media server handling very large files may use XFS. Always consider support and tooling in your distribution, and remember you can mix filesystems across different partitions or logical volumes to match each workload. The core takeaway is to match filesystem features to your operational needs and test before deploying to production.

After creating a partition, you must format it with a filesystem before use. The mkfs tool family applies a chosen filesystem to a partition. For example, to format /dev/sdb1 with ext4 you run mkfs. ext4 on that device. After formatting, use blkid to obtain the device’s UUID and use df -h to confirm mount space once mounted. A concrete example workflow: mkfs. ext4 /dev/sdb1, then sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 to capture the UUID. A common mistake is running mkfs on the wrong partition or an already-mounted partition; formatting will destroy existing data and may break mounted services. Always ensure the target is unmounted and the device is the intended one. Another useful command is tune2fs for ext filesystems to adjust options after formatting. Example: when you make a logical volume in LVM, treat the device path /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv like a partition: format it with mkfs. ext4, create a mount point, and mount it. Takeaway: formatting converts raw partition space into a usable filesystem—do it cautiously and verify identifiers afterward. Formatting a partition and quick mkfs examples means use mkfs to apply a filesystem and blkid to capture uuids; never format the wrong device and avoid formatting mounted devices.. In practical terms, apply a filesystem to a partition and verify with blkid and df. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Mounting attaches a formatted filesystem to a directory so processes can read and write files there. The mount command takes a device path and a mount point. For example, create a directory such as /mnt/data and run mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data to access that filesystem immediately. To unmount use umount and the mount point or device. A frequent issue when unmounting is the target being busy; processes or shells may still have working directories inside the mount point. Use lsof or fuser to find what is holding files open before attempting to unmount. Another practical approach is to stop services that use the mount, close shells, and then unmount. A common misconception is that umount will force-close access; it will not terminate processes by default. Also use df -h to inspect current usage and mounts and check /proc/mounts for the kernel’s view. For temporary mounts this sequence is sufficient, but for persistent mounts you will later add entries to /etc/fstab. Takeaway: mounting is simple, but unmounting safely requires confirmation no process is using the filesystem so you don’t interrupt active work or corrupt data.

The /etc/fstab file configures persistent mounts that the system mounts automatically at boot. Each fstab line includes the device (ideally referenced by UUID), the mount point, filesystem type, mount options, dump, and pass number for fsck. Using UUIDs avoids device-name drift when disks reorder. To get a device UUID use blkid and copy the UUID exactly into fstab. An example fstab entry uses the device UUID, mount point such as /data, ext4 as the filesystem, defaults as options, and 0 2 for dump and fsck order. After editing fstab, always back up the file and test your changes with mount -a to attempt mounting all entries without rebooting. If mount -a returns errors, fix them before reboot. A typical error is a wrong filesystem type or a missing mount point directory. A serious consequence of a bad fstab line is a failed boot that drops the system into emergency mode. The standard recovery is to boot into rescue mode, mount the root volume, and fix or comment out the problematic line. Takeaway: prefer UUIDs, test with mount -a, and keep a backup to safeguard boot behavior.

Logical Volume Management, or LVM, is a layer of abstraction between physical storage and the block devices you format and mount. Instead of fixed partitions, LVM lets you pool physical volumes into a volume group and then carve logical volumes out of that pool. The three core terms to remember are Physical Volume, Volume Group, and Logical Volume. A Physical Volume is a disk or partition initialized for LVM use. You combine one or more PVs into a Volume Group, which acts like a storage pool. From that pool you create Logical Volumes, which behave like regular block devices that you can format and mount. The major benefits are flexibility: you can extend logical volumes without taking them offline, create snapshots for backups, and span storage across multiple disks. A common misconception is that LVM is mandatory; it is optional but valuable when you expect capacity changes. Example: if you have two physical disks, you can add both as PVs to one VG and then create a large LV that uses space from both disks. Takeaway: LVM trades a layer of complexity for powerful online resizing and pooling capabilities—learn the PV→VG→LV relationship to manage it confidently.

This walkthrough covers the exact sequence to create an LVM-backed filesystem you can mount. Start by creating partitions and marking them for LVM, then initialize with pvcreate. For example: sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 initializes two physical volumes. Next create a volume group with sudo vgcreate my_vg /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1. From that group, create a logical volume: sudo lvcreate -L 100G -n user_data_lv my_vg. This yields a device node such as /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv. Format this logical volume with mkfs. ext4, create a mount point, and mount it like any other filesystem. A concrete example: create a 5GB logical volume for a web directory and mount it at /var/www/html_data. A frequent misconception is that you must create equal-sized LVs; you can create many LVs of varying sizes and later extend them as long as there is free space in the VG. Always ensure to run vgdisplay and lvdisplay to confirm capacities before extending or creating LVs. One of LVM’s most valuable features is online resizing. If your volume group has free extents, you can extend a logical volume and then resize its filesystem. The typical sequence is lvextend followed by resize2fs for ext filesystems or xfs_growfs for XFS. For example, to add 50GB to user_data_lv run lvextend -L +50G /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv. After lvextend, resize the filesystem so the OS can use the new space: run sudo resize2fs /dev/my_vg/user_data_lv for ext4. A concrete example: a user_data_lv running out of space can be extended while the system continues to serve files, avoiding lengthy downtime. Misconceptions include assuming every filesystem supports online resize—XFS can only be grown while mounted, and some older filesystems cannot be resized online. Always check free space in the VG with vgs and ensure backups exist before resizing operations. If the VG lacks free space, add a new PV to the VG with pvcreate and vgextend, then repeat the lvextend step. Takeaway: LVM enables safe growth, but the filesystem tool matters; confirm the filesystem type and available VG space before resizing. Storage problems often surface as boot failures, busy unmounts, or lack of space when resizing. The most common boot-time failure arises from an incorrect /etc/fstab line. The system attempts to mount everything in fstab during boot; if an entry references a missing device, wrong UUID, or bad filesystem type, the boot process can drop into emergency mode. The standard fix is to boot from rescue media or use a root shell to mount the root filesystem and edit or comment out the offending line, then test with mount -a. Another frequent issue is attempting to unmount while processes still use the mount point. Use lsof or fuser to identify and stop those processes before unmounting. For LVM, running out of free extents in a VG prevents extending LVs; the remedy is to add a new PV to the VG or free space by shrinking other LVs where possible. A key misconception is assuming that a failed mount at boot always means a corrupted filesystem; often it’s an fstab syntax or device naming problem. Example: after adding a new LV and writing an fstab entry with the wrong UUID, the system fails to boot. Recovery involves fixing fstab, testing with mount -a, and rebooting. Takeaway: careful validation and backups drastically reduce recovery time.

Let’s summarize the essentials you should remember. Partitioning divides a disk into usable sections; always confirm device names and choose GPT for modern large disks. Filesystems are the structures you apply with mkfs—ext4 is a reliable default, XFS fits large-file workloads, and Btrfs provides snapshots but adds complexity. Mounting makes a filesystem accessible; use mount and unmount carefully and check df -h and /proc/mounts. Use UUIDs in /etc/fstab for persistent mounts and always test changes with mount -a to avoid boot-time failures. LVM introduces an abstraction layer: initialize PVs, pool them into VGs, and carve LVs that you format and mount. LVM lets you extend volumes online, create snapshots, and span disks, but requires backups and attention to available VG space. When troubleshooting, check fstab syntax, use lsof or fuser for busy mounts, and expand VGs by adding physical volumes if necessary. These core ideas will help you manage storage reliably and scale it as needs grow.

Keep these three short reminders at hand when you manage storage. First, always confirm device identifiers with lsblk or blkid before partitioning or formatting; a wrong target destroys data. Second, prefer UUIDs for persistent mounts in /etc/fstab and test changes with mount -a so you avoid boot interruptions. Third, use LVM when you expect to resize volumes often—pvcreate, vgcreate, and lvcreate are the basic steps—but keep backups and confirm available VG space before extending. These rules reduce risk and make storage maintenance repeatable across machines. When something goes wrong, step through validation: device names, fstab syntax, running processes holding mounts, and available VG space.
